title: "Skewed and heavy-tailed random effects"

```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  collapse = TRUE,
  comment = "#>"
)
```

```{r setup}
library(rxode2)
```

## Overview

A random effect `eta` is normal, so `cl <- tcl*exp(eta.cl)` gives a
log-normal clearance.  When the population is skewed or heavy tailed, a
shape transform with an estimated shape parameter can replace `eta`
(Petersson et al. 2009):

```r
cl <- tcl*exp(etaBoxCox(eta.cl, lambda))
```

Every transform here keeps `eta = 0` at 0 (so `tcl` is still the typical
value), keeps the rank order of `eta` (so correlations between random effects
are roughly kept), and has a shape value giving the identity (so the shape can
be tested with a likelihood ratio test).

| Function | Transform | Identity at | Changes |
|----|----|----|----|
| `etaBoxCox(eta, lambda)` | `(exp(eta)^lambda - 1)/lambda` | `lambda = 0` | skewness |
| `etaJohnDraper(eta, lambda)` | `sign(eta)*((abs(eta) + 1)^lambda - 1)/lambda` | `lambda = 1` | tails |
| `etaYeoJohnson(eta, lambda)` | `((eta + 1)^lambda - 1)/lambda` for `eta >= 0`, `-((1 - eta)^(2 - lambda) - 1)/(2 - lambda)` below | `lambda = 1` | skewness |
| `etaHeavyTail(eta, theta)` | `eta*abs(eta)^theta` | `theta = 0` | tails (bimodal for `theta < 0`) |
| `etaLogit(eta, theta1, theta2)` | `(expit(logit(theta1) + eta) - theta1)*theta2` | near it at `theta1 = 0.5`, `theta2 = 4` | skewness, width (bounded) |
| `etaSinhAsinh(eta, eps, delta)` | `sinh(delta*asinh(eta) - eps) + sinh(eps)` | `eps = 0`, `delta = 1` | skewness and tails |
| `etaTukeyGH(eta, g, h)` | `(exp(g*eta) - 1)/g*exp(h*eta^2/2)` | `g = 0`, `h = 0` | skewness and tails |

## The transforms in R

Each transform is a C function in the model language, and the R function of
the same name runs that C code, so you can see what a transform does before
putting it in a model:

```{r}
etaBoxCox(c(-1, 0, 1), 0.5)
etaBoxCox(c(-1, 0, 1), 0) # the identity
etaJohnDraper(c(-1, 0, 1), 1) # the identity
```

Applied to normal draws they show the shapes they produce:

```{r eta-shapes, fig.width = 7, fig.height = 3.5}
set.seed(42)
eta <- rnorm(1e5, sd = 0.5)
oldPar <- par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
plot(density(eta), main = "etaBoxCox()", xlim = c(-2.5, 2.5), ylim = c(0, 1.7))
lines(density(etaBoxCox(eta, 1.5)), col = "red")
lines(density(etaBoxCox(eta, -1.5)), col = "blue")
legend("topleft", c("normal", "lambda = 1.5", "lambda = -1.5"),
  col = c("black", "red", "blue"), lty = 1, bty = "n", cex = 0.8
)
plot(density(eta), main = "etaJohnDraper()", xlim = c(-2.5, 2.5), ylim = c(0, 1.7))
lines(density(etaJohnDraper(eta, 2)), col = "red")
lines(density(etaJohnDraper(eta, 0.3)), col = "blue")
legend("topleft", c("normal", "lambda = 2", "lambda = 0.3"),
  col = c("black", "red", "blue"), lty = 1, bty = "n", cex = 0.8
)
par(oldPar)
```

```{r eta-shapes2, fig.width = 7, fig.height = 3.5}
oldPar <- par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
plot(density(eta), main = "etaYeoJohnson()", xlim = c(-2.5, 2.5), ylim = c(0, 1.7))
lines(density(etaYeoJohnson(eta, 1.6)), col = "red")
lines(density(etaYeoJohnson(eta, 0.4)), col = "blue")
legend("topleft", c("normal", "lambda = 1.6", "lambda = 0.4"),
  col = c("black", "red", "blue"), lty = 1, bty = "n", cex = 0.8
)
plot(density(eta), main = "etaHeavyTail()", xlim = c(-2.5, 2.5), ylim = c(0, 1.7))
lines(density(etaHeavyTail(eta, 0.6)), col = "red")
lines(density(etaHeavyTail(eta, -0.4)), col = "blue")
legend("topleft", c("normal", "theta = 0.6", "theta = -0.4"),
  col = c("black", "red", "blue"), lty = 1, bty = "n", cex = 0.8
)
par(oldPar)
```

The two- and three-parameter transforms combine skewness with tails or bounds:

```{r eta-shapes3, fig.width = 7, fig.height = 3.5}
oldPar <- par(mfrow = c(1, 3))
plot(density(eta), main = "etaLogit()", xlim = c(-2.5, 2.5), ylim = c(0, 1.7))
lines(density(etaLogit(eta, 0.5, 4)), col = "red")
lines(density(etaLogit(eta, 0.2, 3)), col = "blue")
legend("topleft", c("normal", "0.5, 4", "0.2, 3"),
  col = c("black", "red", "blue"), lty = 1, bty = "n", cex = 0.8
)
plot(density(eta), main = "etaSinhAsinh()", xlim = c(-2.5, 2.5), ylim = c(0, 1.7))
lines(density(etaSinhAsinh(eta, 0.5, 1)), col = "red")
lines(density(etaSinhAsinh(eta, 0, 1.5)), col = "blue")
legend("topleft", c("normal", "eps = 0.5", "delta = 1.5"),
  col = c("black", "red", "blue"), lty = 1, bty = "n", cex = 0.8
)
plot(density(eta), main = "etaTukeyGH()", xlim = c(-2.5, 2.5), ylim = c(0, 1.7))
lines(density(etaTukeyGH(eta, 1, 0)), col = "red")
lines(density(etaTukeyGH(eta, 0, 0.8)), col = "blue")
legend("topleft", c("normal", "g = 1", "h = 0.8"),
  col = c("black", "red", "blue"), lty = 1, bty = "n", cex = 0.8
)
par(oldPar)
```

The logit transform bounds the random effect to
`(-theta1*theta2, (1 - theta1)*theta2)`, `theta1` setting the skewness and
`theta2` the width.  Sinh-arcsinh is centered here so that `eta = 0` stays at
0; `eps` skews and `delta > 1` gives heavier tails (`delta < 1` lighter).  Tukey's `g` skews like
Box-Cox and `h >= 0` adds tail weight.  The R functions for these have
defaults giving the identity (`eps = 0`, `delta = 1`, `g = 0`, `h = 0`), and
in a model a missing argument takes that default, so
`etaSinhAsinh(eta.cl, delta = d)` expands to `etaSinhAsinh(eta.cl, 0, d)`.

Box-Cox skews: `lambda > 0` gives a long right tail, `lambda < 0` a long
left one.  Yeo-Johnson also skews, the other way round about its identity
(`lambda > 1` a long right tail).  John-Draper and heavy-tailed are symmetric:
`lambda > 1` (John-Draper) or `theta > 0` (heavy-tailed) widens the tails.
`lambda < 1` shortens John-Draper's tails, while `theta < 0` makes the
heavy-tailed transform bimodal; bound `theta` below by 0 to allow only heavier
tails.  A useful starting range is `lambda` in about `(-3, 3)`; `theta` must
stay above -1 for the transform to keep rank order.

## Using them in a model

In a model the transforms take R-style arguments.  A user-defined function
(`rxUdfUi()`) for each one matches the arguments by name, the way R does, and
expands the call into the positional native model function, so the solve runs
C code only:

```{r}
mod <- function() {
  ini({
    tcl <- log(4)
    lcl <- 0.8
    tv <- log(10)
    lv <- 1.5
    eta.cl ~ 0.2
    eta.v ~ 0.1
  })
  model({
    cl <- exp(tcl + etaBoxCox(lambda = lcl, eta = eta.cl))
    v <- exp(tv + etaJohnDraper(eta.v, lambda = lv))
    d / dt(central) <- -cl / v * central
    cp <- central / v
  })
}
ui <- mod()
ui$lstExpr[1:2]
```

The shape (`lcl`, `lv`) is an ordinary theta.  A shaped eta is not
mu-referenced, since it no longer enters as `theta + eta`:

```{r}
ui$nonMuEtas
```

Simulating shows the skewed clearance next to the log-normal one:

```{r cl-sim, fig.width = 7, fig.height = 3.5}
ev <- et(amt = 100) |> et(seq(0, 24, by = 4))
s <- rxSolve(ui, ev, nSub = 2000, returnType = "data.frame")
s0 <- rxSolve(ui |> ini(lcl = 0), ev, nSub = 2000, returnType = "data.frame")
cl <- s$cl[s$time == 0]
cl0 <- s0$cl[s0$time == 0]
plot(density(cl0), main = "Clearance", xlab = "cl", ylim = c(0, 0.35))
lines(density(cl), col = "red")
legend("topright", c("lcl = 0 (log-normal)", "lcl = 0.8"),
  col = c("black", "red"), lty = 1, bty = "n"
)
```

## Exact derivatives

Estimation needs derivatives with respect to both `eta` and the shape.  These
are exact symbolic rules, written so that they stay finite and accurate at the
identity, where the textbook formula is `0/0`.  They are built on
`exprelD(z, n)`, the `n`-th derivative of `(exp(z) - 1)/z`:

```{r}
rxFromSE("Derivative(etaBoxCox(eta, lambda), lambda)")
etaBoxCox(0.5, c(-1e-8, 0, 1e-8))
exprelD(0, 0:3)
```

The derivatives of `etaJohnDraper()` and `etaYeoJohnson()` with respect to
`eta` are written without `sign()`, so they are 1 at `eta = 0` rather than 0.
`etaHeavyTail()`'s derivatives use `absPowLog(x, p, k)`, which is
`abs(x)^p*log(abs(x))^k` with its limit at `x = 0`; its slope at `eta = 0` is
0 for `theta > 0`, so a random effect near 0 moves the parameter little.

## Reference

Petersson KJ, Hanze E, Savic RM, Karlsson MO.  Semiparametric distributions
with estimated shape parameters.  Pharm Res.  2009;26(9):2174-85.

Jones MC, Pewsey A.  Sinh-arcsinh distributions.  Biometrika.
2009;96(4):761-80.
